point: Norway's grid is regulated and hydro dominated, and reservoir storage gives dispatchable capacity that becomes more valuable as wind and solar grow.
Flexibility means adapting to supply and demand changes, and variable renewables raise the need for it.
Rising demand projections and intermittent supply call for a flexible, well-dimensioned grid with smart metering.
Too little flexibility forces curtailment of renewables, which hurts emissions goals and project revenues and may deter investors.
Flexibility used to come from supply-side generators with inertia, and inverter-based renewables erode that inertia and create a need for new measures.
Demand-side management is spreading as a balancing tool, helped by smart meters and by power-intensive loads that raise prosumer influence.
Demand-side strategies shave peaks and move load, and peak shaving, valley filling and load shifting are the relevant ones here.
Prosumers need information, engagement and aligned incentives to provide flexibility, and studies show pricing signals and coordinated scheduling help.
Distributed flexibility resources such as batteries, EV charging and curtailable loads enable demand-side flexibility, and the section reviews those relevant to the case.
Batteries are purely flexible assets that shift energy in time, and one study shows they cut cost and grid import with renewables.
EV charging can shift load to cheap hours and save money, and the thesis treats vehicle-to-grid and grid-to-vehicle charging.
Bidirectional chargers let EV batteries behave like stationary storage and exploit price differences.
Van et al. show predictive control of EV charging achieves peak shaving, with vehicle-to-grid beating grid-to-vehicle.
Curtailment is defined here as cutting consumption of non-critical loads rather than cutting generation.
Building thermal mass makes heating a flexibility source, but studies find it needs good forecasts and suits fast reserves better than bulk shifting.
Aggregating prosumers overcomes market size barriers and brings cost and variability reductions, though flexibility markets were designed for large actors.
Demand response splits into price-based and incentive-based programs, and the section defines each.
Flexibility pays more where prices vary frequently, as a study of price variability and prosumer savings confirms.
Dynamic and capacity-based grid tariffs give better flexibility incentives than static volumetric ones, according to Norwegian-adjacent and Danish studies.
Feed-in and grid tariff design shape incentives for local storage and PV, and the new Norwegian dynamic tariff may favour load shifting.
Incentive-based programs add value without penalising non-participation, unlike price-based ones.
Incentive programs rely on contracts of varied obligation, and one study shows incentive and penalty levels drive revenue and load outcomes.
Frequency reserve markets are a new and important incentive program, and the thesis focuses on prosumer participation in one.
Falling system inertia from renewables creates both a need for fast frequency reserves and an opening for prosumers.
Norwegian reserve products respond in sequence to frequency drops, and their size thresholds hinder small prosumers unless loads are aggregated.
Aggregation is a feasible and already practised route into reserve markets, though it needs advanced bidding models.
The fastest reserve is least disruptive and fits the campus data, so the thesis studies that market.
Statnett opened a commercial fast reserve market in 2022 with two contract types, seasonal timing and published volumes and prices.
The reserve product has support durations, activation limits and recovery rules that participants must meet.
Small resources must be pooled to reach the minimum size, and little work exists on neighbourhood batteries and EVs in the fast reserve.
Karbouj et al. argue demand response, storage and PV can give fast frequency support if control is fast enough.
Kushwaha et al. show aggregated EV scheduling gives sizeable fast reserve capacity and lowers curtailment, without studying individual chargers.
Stationary batteries resemble vehicle-to-grid EVs but differ in charge needs and constraints, and research on their fast reserve use is scarce.
Battery wear costs matter but studies find EV reserve provision still pays, particularly with lithium-ion batteries.
Thermostatic loads suit fast reserves because of thermal inertia, and studies find they earn revenue and ease system balance.
The thesis studies stacked prosumer flexibility with fast reserve participation, a topic with little prior research, and reviews the closest studies.
Backe et al. find coordinated demand response beats individual response under capacity tariffs on the same campus, and this thesis extends their scope.
Ahčin et al. analyse four battery demand response cases in Norway but ignore combining mechanisms.
Ahčin et al. find tariff-only battery cases unprofitable while reserve market participation makes batteries profitable, so stacking helps investment.
Firoozi et al. show a local energy community raises profit by providing slower manual reserves.
Firoozi's work looks at the aggregate community, whereas this thesis studies a single prosumer and the fast reserve.
The thesis adds an analysis of individual prosumer operation with fast reserve participation.
No study has examined how fast reserve access changes prosumer costs, so the thesis builds a cost-minimising model on campus data.
A fragment of a research question asks how to achieve the highest economic value from flexibility resources.
